poiPLY-desc:
Polystralia is the bloc of the southern seas. It joins the Nusantaran Association, the Federation of Australasia and the corporate republic of Westralia, and its reach runs from the drowned archipelagos of the old Indonesia to the islands of the Pacific. No region on Earth was hit harder by the rising seas, and few have kept more of their wealth.

That wealth lies underground. Polystralia is one of the world's great quarries, rich in iron above all, along with coal, bauxite, nickel, lithium, manganese, cobalt, titanium and uranium, and its exports keep it afloat while so many others have drowned. Who profits is another question. In Australasia, decades of comfortable rule have blended the old parties into a single corrupt establishment. In Westralia, the corporations own the state outright. In Nusantara, millions of people forced from their homelands by the tides are still looking for somewhere to stand.

Nusantara is the rising power of the three. It has quickly closed the gap with Australasia, and Canberra's old dominance of the south is no longer taken for granted. The question for Polystralia is whether a bloc built on resources and refugees can hold together once the islands it was meant to protect are gone.
poiPLY001-desc: The Pacific was hit hardest of all by the rising seas, yet Nusantara is something of a rising power in the region. It has quickly closed the gap with Australasia, though not without internal conflicts of its own. So many of its communities have been forced from their traditional homelands by the tides that resettlement, and the question of who gets to stay where, shapes nearly everything its government does.
poiPLY002-desc: For all the chaos that has wracked the world, Australasia's land, educated population and natural resources have let it weather the crises with relative prosperity. Deep-rooted political and environmental problems remain, and not everyone has prospered equally, but its exports have kept it afloat while so many others have drowned. Compared with other nations that survived the Dark Days, its people enjoy a precious semblance of normalcy, and some pride in how lucky they are to live there.
poiPLY003-desc:
Even so, Australia and its neighbours were dealt tremendous blows by the Great Mistake. The iconic coastal cities are long underwater, and with them the infrastructure that once supported most of the population. Inland communities suffer multi-year droughts broken only by devastating storms and flash floods. Long-touted technological fixes have helped little and cost much, aid budgets are stretched when they exist at all, and the bush is growing underpoliced and dangerous to cross without protection.

The armed forces are no better. The coup in the old United States left Australia without its main defence partner. The air force still relies on old American imports, the navy's next-generation ships are last-generation by the time they launch, and the army has become a glorified disaster relief agency, rushing from one catastrophe to the next.
poiPLY004-desc: Since the Federation of Australasia was founded, Australia has dominated its smaller partners politically and economically. Given its population and landmass that is no surprise, but many in the Pacific feel they are not getting a fair go. The Federation's wealth stays in Australia, while shrinking aid budgets hit the islands hardest, just as rising seas and extreme weather tear apart what is left of their infrastructure. New Zealand is increasingly the voice of its smaller neighbours, and without action the inequality will only fester.
poiPLY005-desc:
Ever since the Dark Days, when Australia's establishment parties realised their power was all but permanent, laziness and lax government crept onto the parliament floor. Corruption has blended the competing parties into what is known simply as the Federalist establishment, and little changes whoever is in office.

Rhonda Campbell's father led the Federation decades ago, and his name gave her career an edge. When she won the 2199 election, she discovered how ineffectual the government's inner workings truly are: pointless infighting, incompetent management and corrupt deals made in broad daylight. Educated but inexperienced, she found herself not the head of a great Pacific federation but a scapegoat, a figure for the corporations and the masses to point at. She still hopes for some real liberty, though only so much can be done with a knife at your back. With masterful navigation of the political minefield, and a ripe enough opportunity, she may yet become a legend of Oceania.
poiPLY006-desc:
Ian Forscyth could be condensed into the archetypal Australian man: fierce, brave and always good-humoured. Beneath the smile is an idealist who just wants his old friends and family back. Raised among the rural communities of central New South Wales, he hoped for a simple pastoral life of songs and stories, Waltzing Matilda and Ned Kelly, a fondness the newer urban arrivals met with little enthusiasm.

He believes the government is too corrupt and too far gone for reform, and that the country's tattered social fabric will unravel into anarchy before the Federalists even draft a proposal for change. His answer is as simple as it is paradoxical: look to the past and to the future at once. He calls for the values from the far side of the Great Mistake, from a time when "a fair go" was more than a snide comment and mateship forged bonds that weathered fire and flood, to be fused with the new into a radically different system. Nostalgic, possibly. Audacious, absolutely.
poiPLY007-desc:
Long marginalised in Australian politics, First Nations communities were among the hardest hit by the Great Mistake. Torres Strait Islanders watched their homes sink beneath the waves, and Aboriginal Australians found themselves at the bottom of the list for disaster relief. With nobody else to turn to, they turned to each other, building networks to coordinate aid and, as the bush became harder to police, militias to defend themselves. From them the Bushranger movement was born. The name was meant as an insult. They kept it.

Sarah Gurruwiwi's origins are a mystery, even, she likes to joke, to herself; she was separated from her birth family in the botched evacuation of her town in the Northern Territory. After a walkabout across the lands and communities of the north, she led a campaign to reach the people the government ignored: the starving were taught to farm bush tucker, the threatened were given adaptation plans drawn from ancient knowledge of the land, and the militias rallied to poor communities when bandits drew near. The movement spread to the Pacific Islands and became a small but firm voice for the underclasses in Australasian politics.

Its unity is shaky. Some Bushrangers believe society can only survive by restoring its connection to the land and the past, others that new technologies must be embraced to protect what is left. Now elderly, Aunty Gurruwiwi is an experienced arbiter, but with her own sons on opposite sides, she is struggling to hold her movement together.
poiPLY008-desc:
The idea of an independent Western Australia predates the Great Mistake, and it found new life after it. Corporate interests joined in, and cut a deal with a desperate Australasia: massive financial and economic support in exchange for an independent Westralia. Once it was founded, the young country was firmly, if discreetly, under corporate control. The politicians are in their pockets, the police at their beck and call, and the whole country is theirs to profit from. The deal improved Australasia's finances, but it has emboldened radical movements across the Federation, many of which now field militias of their own.

Westralia is a world leader in raw materials and manufactured goods, with only the most token conservation standing between the corporations and the riches underground, and even that exists only to keep agriculture profitable. Visitors are advised to buy a breathing mask on arrival.
poiPLY009-desc:
Somewhere in the bleak and barren skyline of Kalgoorlie sits Claudius Reid, the unwilling "president" of the Westralian Republic. Born to a wealthy British family with strong business ties, he first tried his hand at British politics. He was sharp, but his lack of charm and persuasion killed that dream. Lost and alone, he learned through his corporate connections that a new Westralian president was to be chosen in secret, moved to Westralia, seized the chance and, to his delight, won.

Then the trap closed. He was sworn in above a weary crowd, with no applause and no ceremony. Now he sits in his black-walled office, pondering and wasting away, the optimism that once drove him gone. When he can summon the energy to look down at the citizens below, he sees the same gutted husks, coughing and choking at their own misfortune, oblivious to the helpless leader above them.
poiPLY010-desc:
The Free Drones take their name from an insult. A mining magnate, caught on a hot mic, called Westralia's workers mindless rabble buzzing like drones in a beehive. The corporate media tried to bury it, and it might have faded had the largest alliance of the country's embattled unions not taken the name for themselves. With every scandal over worker mistreatment and every accident caused by lax protections, the Free Drones grow, and suppression has only backed them into a corner where many believe violence is the last way to be heard.

Their leader is Arthur Donaldson. He won a mining scholarship to a dual degree in geology and engineering and went straight into the mines, an unremarkable path by Westralian standards. But he grew up amid the poverty of the working-class towns, haunted union meetings and strikes from a young age, and holds a worldview of implacable class struggle that can only end with the destruction of the oppressors. He leads the largest union coalition in Australian history with fiery speeches and strong-arm tactics. Even some of his own followers think he may be unhinged, and he may be the one spark that sets the country alight.
